pitch_detail.notes: A chimney system leads up into a cave under the start of a steep flare. Gear is reasonable for the difficulty. Several bulges with poor footholds and workable snice for the tools are the hard parts.

Excellent mixed climbing: stem and chimney up the flare on good rock gear, then move onto ice, tunnel through a curtain and surmount another steep bulge. The belay is the shared midpoint ledge with the neighbouring Fossen Falls line.
A thin start off the ledge gains a narrow steep pillar pouring from a groove. Rock gear turns up now and then. Belay in a sheltered spot beneath the roof.

Continue on ice until it ends below the roof. Clip a bolt, then aid through or pull hard on the holds. Three bolts and a cam cover the roof. Above it the going eases only slightly and gear is absent for a few moves. Belay on the obvious ledge. This roof has not been freed yet.
Follow the ramp-like corner up and left. At the fork keep left to the bolted anchor on a pedestal, which is also where the rappels down Fossen Falls begin.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches; the text gives no per-pitch grades or lengths so none are given. No rappel table (only a single rappel onto the neighbouring line is mentioned).

pitch_detail.notes: Steep rolling ice leads to the foot of the cliff.
A long pitch of good ice up to the base of the fork.
Steep, sustained ice up the left fork to the top; shorter than the first two.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches with the stated grades; protection is screws and threads, not per pitch.

pitch_detail.notes: A stepped, partly consolidated curtain of ice about 15 m high, then another 15 m of snow to the foot of a deep slot.
The serious climbing begins: a steep 20 m heap of frozen gravel with poor protection, then enjoyable ice, finishing at a belay in a cave at the back of the slot. Marked R for the thin gear.
Steep thin ice followed by bumps up to a deep cave at the back of the slot. Big ice hangs overhead.

Ice drips through a wide cleft in a 5 m roof and barely reaches the ground. Climb a fragile icicle as high as it allows to reach thick ice at the cleft, traverse left carefully placing screws high, then at the lip reach round to the ice in front and move up while stemming on rock. Commit to the overhanging ice, which turns vertical after a few metres and relaxes over the last 30 m.
About 30 m of steep ice reaches a shoulder; belay on the right.
Climb to a belay on the left.
Very steep, sustained ice for about 45 m before the angle relaxes for the last 15 m. Wet, with odd ice formations.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches. The long approach traverse with bolted running belays and two short rappels is not put in the table.

pitch_detail.notes: Very wet. Start at the left edge and take the driest line to a sheltered belay directly behind the pillar.

Go around to the front of the pillar, about 1 m across, and climb dead vertical ice that trembles underfoot. The pillar stands free for 25 m, merges with the upper curtain, and 35 m higher the ice lies back to easy ground.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches. The pillar is often unformed or broken off.

pitch_detail.notes: A clear hand crack leads to a small bulge, then a 5.10b crack continues to a belay where the other cracks are visible to the left.
Stay in the same crack for about 20 ft, then face climb left about 10 ft to a second crack and again to a third. Belay short to limit rope drag.
Follow the crack as far as it goes; sustained.
Finish the crack, then move right before it dies to rough flakes at the edge of a roof atop a slab (5.9). Strong climbers may link pitches 2 to 4 into three, which takes a lot of gear.
The next three pitches are on the east side of the buttress. Follow grooves, corners and flakes straight up and slightly left.
More 5.7 corners lead to a 30 ft 10b crack right of the obvious off-width.
Mid-fifth class, blocky terrain with good exposure. Watch for drag.
Fourth class with short low fifth steps.
Fourth class, then third class to the summit.
Up a runout diagonal crack to a loose, sloppy ledge.
Traverse left aiming for the hand crack in the roof.
Go straight up, or traverse down and right until loose cracks lead to the base of the obvious chimney-corner.
Straight up the corner to a sheltered alcove; good climbing.
Continue up the corner to a good ledge with an undercling crack to the right.
Go up and left, place gear, downclimb below the belayer and traverse left beneath a small roof to a finger crack in a corner. Follow the cracks to a good corner crack and a belay ledge.
Climb above the belay to a good ledge, then a short cruxy corner leads to easy ground into the forest.

rappel_detail.notes: Reached by following the obvious ledge climber's left from the top. Full 60 m rope rappel.
Full 60 m rappel that also crosses the gully.
Full 60 m rappel down to a grassy slope. Hike down to the next tree.

review.changed: Wrote 7 pitches and a 4-station rappel table from the listed descent (60 m ropes).

pitch_detail.notes: Starts in a narrow gully that widens. The belay stance is awkward because it sits on a steeply angled avalanche path: pack the snow down and build an ice screw anchor.
A gentle waterfall with snow before and after. Belay from the tree on the right beyond the gully, which carries old tat in poor shape, half buried in ice. Rappel from this tree.
The best pitch, with several comfortable landings on the way up to a tree with tat on the left.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches; the text grades none of them separately so no grade is given. No rappel table (one tree rappel mentioned).

pitch_detail.notes: Scramble a short ramp on the left to the crack. A big flake is fun to climb; when the crack pinches, tiptoe round it on a left-hand ramp and seam, then a powerful undercling or sidepull move reaches ledges and ramps up to a tree belay. A small redirect left of the tree makes the top belay nicer.

A low crux up a steep flared crack, then ledges. Follow the crack, wandering slightly, to a large sloping ledge with a good off-width in its left corner. Build a gear belay at the base of the off-width (medium or larger gear and a nut); a tree is a possible alternative. Escape past this point needs double ropes.

Walk to the right side of the ledge and consider a redirect. Climb blocky ground, staying right, into a chimney and leave your pack hanging below you. The original line weaves between two chockstones; larger climbers can go outside both. Beware loose blocks. Scramble the gully, then veer up and left to the second tree for the belay. Rope drag is a concern.

One or two short pitches: climb the boulder above and right of the tree, bushwhack through dense trees up and right, then cut left to exit into scrambly terrain. A class 3-4 ridge scramble then reaches the summit.

review.changed: Wrote P1-P3 plus one linked entry for the 1-2 short pitches described. Lengths for P1-P3 come from the stated 35-40 m range, entered as 37 (approximate).

pitch_detail.notes: A short, wider and easier opening section leads to excellent but dirty hand jamming past a small roof. Belay on a grassy ledge. Needs cleaning before a redpoint; moss and heather in the crack were aided through.

Estimated length. Go up until the crack thins, then veer left over slab for easier climbing; a bit runout. Regain the crack, move left to a small right-facing undercling corner, climb it, pass dense vegetation and loose blocks, and belay on a ledge. Could be split in two short pitches.
Estimated length. Go left and up on a traversing crack to a slab above rockfall scars. Climb the easy featured slab, which takes gear in cracks, to a tree above and right.

Estimated length. The key pitch. From the tree go left then up to the headwall of steep splitter cracks. The left crack is about 5.10+ to the horizontal break and likely 5.11 through steep fingers; the 5 m crux was aided. Near the top move right and mantle to a big ledge.
Estimated length. Move up and left through easier, varied terrain to the top of the wall, where technical climbing ends.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches; lengths are estimates and are flagged as such in the notes.
review.other_findings: The route has only been done as 5.10 A0; the stored 5.11 is the projected free grade, not a contradiction.

pitch_detail.notes: Start from the orange ledge up a featured slab to a high bolt in line with the bushy ledge. Two bolts plus gear.

Straight up to a bolt, trend left past another and climb the leftmost of two layback flakes, then trend up right to the small buttress (avoid the left-facing corner system on the far left). Bolts and gear; save a .4 and .5 for the top. Climb out left round the tree to the belay on George Ledge.
Face climb past three bolts to a right-trending diagonal crack, step left to a bolt above it, continue past another, then straight up and left round the corner to easier ground and a stance.

Climb the left-facing corner with a crack to a bolt, step right to a wide flake with good gear above, then follow crack pods up and slightly right (the hard part, good gear). Go to a bolt above a small roof and trend right past two more bolts to a ledge.

Layback the crack left of the belay, break right toward the roof, pass it by a left-leaning crack and step left onto a small ledge to a bolt. Follow the steepening bolt line; belay on the right by the roof.

A short, steep sport pitch: climb up right into the overhanging crest of the wave. Powerful and exposed. It can be worked by fixing the rope and walking back via the variation. Variation (5.8, one bolt): escape left to the ridge, protected by one bolt, with gear belays on the ridge.

review.changed: Wrote all 6 pitches. No rappel table (rappelling from every pitch on two 60 m ropes is a general statement).

pitch_detail.notes: Starts at the base of a shallow corner crack on the west face. Follow the crack to a bolted station in a shallow dish; a rappel back to the ledge at the base is possible.

Continue up the crack past two pitons, the first crux, to a small ledge about 40 m up beneath a mossy steep section. Move left to a left-facing flake that cannot be seen from the corner and continue to a bolted ledge belay.

Step right into the corner crack and climb past the flaring corner, the second crux. Stem up steep ground to an alcove-chimney behind a left-facing flake, squeeze through, then step right to a small ledge with a bolted belay.

Step right into a left-facing corner and follow it to the top of the headwall, then up and slightly right through broken cracks. When the angle lessens look right to an obvious belay ledge under a small roof.
Pull through the roof, then slabs with short vertical steps until the ground eases. Scramble easy fifth class to the top.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches (P1 taken from the access paragraph). Rappelling from the top of P3 needs double 60 m ropes; no full rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Thin right-facing flakes lead to a large ledge.
Traverse up and left to a broad ledge.
Large left-facing flakes and corners lead to a jam crack in the headwall, ending in a comfortable alcove.
Steep rock on positive holds past a bolt gains the long layback and finger crack above.
Traverse right to the bolted large left-facing corner. The hard section is short; pull on the bolts if needed (5.9 C1).
Climb the steep roof above on positive holds.
Ramble to the top.

review.changed: The text numbers only P1-P5, with the last label holding three segments (crux corner, roof, ramble); these are split as 5, 6, 7 to match the stored count of 7. Medium confidence on that split. No lengths given.

pitch_detail.notes: Low-angle rock to a grassy ledge, then the obvious corner below the main arete. Semi-hanging belay beneath a small roof.
Squeeze through a roof chimney and continue up the corner to a good belay below a big roof and steep section.
An easy line through the roof, past a second small roof, to a steep crack at the base of the arete; step right to a bolted belay.
Step right of the arete onto the face and up an obvious crack to steep, shallow flaring corner cracks (first crux). Belay just below a single bolt, which can be added to the small-gear anchor.
Continue up the face crack through a steep corner crack, past two more bolts and a small roof (second crux), to easy ground and the summit. Put extenders on the cams in the roof to limit drag.
